strengths: Very simple and practical idea: applying an elementwise sign-power transform to gradients before the base optimizer is easy to implement, has negligible reported step-time overhead, and is compatible with AdamW, Muon, and blockwise learning rates.

The empirical section is broader than many optimizer papers: experiments cover dense LLaMA-style models, Qwen2MoE models, C4 and OpenWebText, cosine and WSD schedules, model sizes up to 2B, downstream zero-shot evaluation, clipping-order ablations, batch-size sensitivity, and some multi-seed checks.

The paper makes a useful attempt to connect the empirical behavior to gradient-noise regimes, including an illustrative analysis explaining why p>1 may help in high-noise settings and p<1 may help with larger batches.
Presentation is generally clear, with readable algorithms, experimental settings, and appendices listing model configurations and learning-rate grids.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are stronger than the evidence fully supports. Most headline LLM/MoE results appear to be single runs, with multi-seed validation only for two small dense settings; the downstream gains are modest, and the reported scaling-law/FLOP savings are not accompanied by enough fitting methodology or uncertainty.

Reproducibility is incomplete: I did not find a code release, full command/config dump, data preprocessing details, exact random seeds for all runs, or complete numerical tables for the plotted curves. This matters because optimizer gains at these scales can be sensitive to implementation details.

Originality is useful but incremental. The appendix acknowledges close relation to the Powerball method; the main novelty is applying and validating the idea in modern LLM pretraining and considering p>1/noise regimes, rather than introducing a fundamentally new optimizer principle.

The theory is only partially aligned with the empirical method. The convergence guarantees are for AdagradPower under strong and somewhat specialized low-/high-noise assumptions, while the main method is AdamWPower/MuonPower in transformer pretraining. The assumptions also effectively encode favorable gradient-noise behavior, so the results are more explanatory than independently predictive.

The paper repeatedly suggests scalability to larger models and special promise for MoE/WSD training, but experiments stop at relatively small pretraining scales by current LLM standards and use short context lengths for C4, so the extrapolation should be framed more cautiously.

Limitations and ethics are treated briefly. The conclusion notes future work, but there is little direct discussion of failure modes, sensitivity to epsilon/gradient scale, interaction with mixed precision or distributed training, or cases where the transform may harm training.

strengths: The proposed GradPower transformation is simple, easy to implement, and potentially practical: applying sign(g)|g|^p before the optimizer is genuinely lightweight and compatible with AdamW, Muon, and blockwise LR variants.

The manuscript evaluates the idea on several language-model pretraining settings, including dense LLaMA-style models, Qwen2MoE models, C4/OpenWebText, cosine and WSD schedules, and model sizes up to 2B parameters. This breadth is a positive aspect relative to many optimizer papers.
The appendix provides useful implementation details such as model configurations, learning-rate grids, batch sizes, sequence lengths, and some additional checks over random seeds and beta parameters.
The paper acknowledges related sign-power methods such as Powerball and distinguishes the LLM-pretraining/adaptive-optimizer setting, which helps clarify the intended contribution.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are overextended relative to the evidence. Many reported gains are very small, e.g. downstream average improves only from 47.72 to 48.26 and one task gets worse, yet the paper repeatedly claims strong acceleration, improved scaling laws, and large FLOP savings without sufficiently detailed statistical support.

Most large-scale experiments appear to be single-run curves. The multi-seed validation is limited to two small LLaMA settings, while the main claims about 1B-2B models, MoE models, WSD schedules, Muon compatibility, and scaling-law compute savings lack variance estimates or significance tests.

The fairness of optimizer comparison is not fully convincing. AdamWPower mostly reuses AdamW learning rates and tunes p once, but the paper does not adequately explore whether AdamW, Muon, or other baselines could close the small gaps through comparable tuning of learning rate, schedule, clipping, weight decay, epsilon, or beta parameters. The beta sweep is only one OpenWebText setting and finds a very small gap of about 0.004 loss.

The scaling-law/FLOP-saving claims are insufficiently documented. Figure 1 reports dramatic labels such as 0.157x, 0.162x, and 0.258x FLOPs, but the manuscript does not give enough methodology, uncertainty, or extrapolation details to make these claims reliable.

The theoretical analysis does not strongly support the paper's main AdamW/LLM claims. The convergence result is for AdagradPower, not AdamWPower; the assumptions largely encode favorable alignment properties of powered gradients; and the comparison sometimes changes the norm or hides constants, limiting the practical interpretability of the claimed acceleration.

Originality is limited. The paper itself notes close similarity to the Powerball method, and the main novelty is applying a known sign-power transformation to modern LLM optimizers with p sometimes above 1. This may be useful, but it is not a conceptually deep advance unless the empirical evidence is much more conclusive.

The discussion of limitations is thin. Important limitations such as lack of code release, single-seed large runs, sensitivity to epsilon/gradient scale, limited downstream evaluation, and uncertainty in scaling-law extrapolations are not clearly acknowledged.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and architectures are described, but there is no apparent code link, no exact training/evaluation scripts, no raw logs, and no details sufficient to independently verify the claimed scaling-law fits or FLOP savings. For a compute-heavy optimizer paper, this is a material weakness.

The presentation is generally understandable, but it tends to use strong language such as 'consistently', 'remarkable', and 'strictly accelerates' in places where the evidence is modest or indirect. This makes the claims feel less calibrated than they should for an ICML main-track submission.

strengths: The paper proposes a very simple and practical gradient sign-power transformation that can be inserted before existing optimizers with minimal implementation burden and negligible reported overhead.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for an optimizer paper: dense LLaMA and Qwen2MoE models from 66M to 2B parameters, C4 and OpenWebText, cosine and warmup-stable-decay schedules, plus compatibility tests with Blockwise LR and Muon.

Results are consistent and practically meaningful: AdamWPower lowers terminal validation loss across the main settings, improves zero-shot average performance for the 2B LLaMA model, and appears especially helpful for MoE and WSD training where optimizer robustness matters.

The paper includes useful ablations on the exponent p, clipping order, batch size/noise, limited multi-seed runs, and momentum-parameter tuning, which makes the central empirical story more convincing than a single benchmark comparison.

The theoretical sections give a plausible mechanism connecting gradient noise, the optimal exponent, and adaptive optimizer behavior; while not fully matching AdamW pretraining, they help explain why p>1 can be beneficial in high-noise regimes and p<1 in lower-noise regimes.
Presentation is generally clear, with a readable method, explicit experimental settings, and an honest note relating the method to prior Powerball work.
weaknesses: Originality is somewhat moderated by the close relationship to the Powerball method and other sign-power transformations. The paper’s main novelty is the LLM-pretraining setting, p>1/noise analysis, and extensive optimizer integration rather than a wholly new transformation.

The theoretical guarantees are for simplified settings, especially toy one-dimensional AdamW behavior and AdagradPower rather than AdamWPower or MuonPower. The assumptions are strong, so the theory should be viewed as explanatory rather than decisive support for the main LLM claims.

Reproducibility is only partial: the paper gives model/hyperparameter details, but I did not find a code release or exact training recipe sufficient to independently reproduce the large-scale runs. Many major experiments appear to be single runs, with multi-seed evidence only on smaller subsets.

Several important results are shown mainly as plots without comprehensive numeric tables, confidence intervals, or compute-normalized summaries. This makes it harder to judge effect sizes, statistical reliability, and scaling-law fits precisely.

The baseline tuning protocol may slightly favor the proposed method’s narrative: AdamW learning rates are tuned, but AdamWPower largely reuses those settings plus a p tuned on one small run. This is practically appealing, but a fuller comparison would include stronger retuning or compute-matched hyperparameter budgets for both sides.

The limitations and ethics discussion are thin. The paper mentions future work on MoE/WSD mechanisms and dynamic p, but does not deeply discuss failure modes, sensitivity across training stages, possible instability from transforming very small gradients, or the societal implications of cheaper LLM pretraining.
